signal.title: Per-packet service LB: embedded packet inside ICMP Fragmentation Needed is not reverse-translated, breaking PMTUD for ClusterIP flows
signal.text: ## Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues Closest matches found: #39773 (host firewall / DNAT reply misrouting in tunnel mode) and #46993 (PMTU handling for L4 services, DSR/Maglev) — neither describes this: the outer header of an ICMP error is reverse-translated for a ClusterIP flow while the embedded original packet is not. ## What happened? For pod→ClusterIP traffic handled by the per-packet service load balancer (socket LB disabled), when a hop behind the backend pod returns **ICMP type 3 code 4 (Fragmentation Needed)**, Cilium reverse-translates the **outer** IP header of the ICMP error (source becomes the ClusterIP), but the **embedded original packet inside the ICMP payload keeps the post-DNAT tuple** (backend pod IP / target port instead of ClusterIP / service port). The client kernel matches ICMP errors to sockets by the embedded tuple. The socket is connected to `ClusterIP:port`, the embedded packet says `podIP:targetPort`, so the error is discarded. Path MTU discovery never happens: the client retransmits the same oversized DF segment until the connection times out. Any TCP flow whose segments exceed the bottleneck MTU black-holes; small requests work, which makes this very confusing to diagnose (it presents as "TLS handshakes and SSH hang through ClusterIP, everything works via pod IP"). tcpdump on the client pod (socket connected to ClusterIP `10.100.170.252:8080`, backend pod `10.244.27.179`): ``` IP 10.100.170.252 > 10.244.29.246: ICMP 10.244.27.179 unreachable - need to frag (mtu 800), length 556 IP 10.244.29.246.34672 > 10.244.27.179.8080: Flags [P.], ... length 1555 POST / HTTP/1.1 Host: 10.100.170.252:8080 ``` Outer source is the ClusterIP (translated), the embedded destination is still the pod IP (not translated). The same request sent directly to the pod IP receives an identical ICMP whose embedded tuple matches the socket, the kernel lowers the path MTU, retransmits smaller segments and the request completes in ~2 ms. Via the ClusterIP the client retransmits the full-size segment 7 times and times out. Expected behavior: the embedded packet should be reverse-translated together with the outer header (destination rewritten back to `ClusterIP:servicePort`), which is what netfilter's SNAT/DNAT does for ICMP errors (RFC 5508 §4.2 semantics). Datapath config where this was hit: `routing-mode=tunnel`, `tunnel-protocol=vxlan`, `kube-proxy-replacement=true`, `bpf-lb-sock=false` (per-packet service translation), `enable-bpf-masquerade` unset (iptables masquerade), host firewall enabled. Real-world trigger was a Tailscale egress proxy pod (tun MTU 1280) fronted by a ClusterIP Service, but the repro below is self-contained. ## How can we reproduce the issue? Backend pod that forwards into a low-MTU link inside its own netns (stand-in for any VPN/tunnel proxy pod): ```bash kubectl run repro-backend --image=nicolaka/netshoot --restart=Never \ --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"repro-backend","image":"nicolaka/netshoot","command":["sleep","1800"],"securityContext":{"privileged":true}}]}}' kubectl exec repro-backend -- bash -c ' ip netns add inner ip link add veth0 type veth peer name veth1 ip link set veth1 netns inner ip addr add 192.168.99.1/30 dev veth0 ip link set veth0 mtu 800 up ip netns exec inner ip addr add 192.168.99.2/30 dev veth1 ip netns exec inner ip link set veth1 mtu 1500 up ip netns exec inner ip link set lo up ip netns exec inner ip route add default via 192.168.99.1 sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 8080 -j DNAT --to-destination 192.168.99.2:8080 ip netns exec inner sh -c "cd /tmp && nohup python3 -m http.server 8080 >/dev/null 2>&1 &"' kubectl expose pod repro-backend --name repro-svc --port 8080 ``` Client pod **on a different node** (so the flow crosses the tunnel): ```bash kubectl run repro-client --image=nicolaka/netshoot --restart=Never --command -- sleep 1800 kubectl exec repro-client -- bash -c ' head -c 1400 /dev/zero | tr "\0" "A" > /tmp/big tcpdump -nn -v -i eth0 icmp & sleep 2 curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "via ClusterIP: %{http_code} %{time_total}s\n" -m 8 -X POST --data-binary @/tmp/big http://<CLUSTER_IP>:8080/ || true curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "via pod IP: %{http_code} %{time_total}s\n" -m 8 -X POST --data-binary @/tmp/big http://<POD_IP>:8080/ || true' ``` Result: - via ClusterIP: `000 8.0s` (timeout) — ICMP arrives with outer src = ClusterIP but embedded dst = pod IP, client keeps retransmitting the 1450-byte segment; - via pod IP: `501 0.002s` (instant; 501 is just python http.server rejecting POST) — same ICMP, embedded tuple matches the socket, PMTUD works. ## Cilium Version ``` Client: 1.17.3 3993bd06 2025-04-09T16:59:44+00:00 go version go1.23.8 linux/amd64 Daemon: 1.17.3 3993bd06 2025-04-09T16:59:44+00:00 go version go1.23.8 linux/amd64 ``` ## Kernel Version ``` Linux 6.8.0-90-generic x86_64 (Ubuntu 24.04.2 LTS) ``` ## Kubernetes Version ``` v1.31.1 (kubeadm) ``` ## Regression Unknown — first noticed on 1.17.3; we have no data from earlier versions. ## Sysdump Not attached (production cluster); can provide targeted `cilium-dbg monitor` captures or specific map dumps on request. ## Relevant log output `cilium-dbg monitor -vv` on the client node during a stalled TLS handshake through a ClusterIP (backend is a proxy pod with tun MTU 1280; service `10.105.148.60:443` → `10.244.2.99:10162`): ```shell Policy verdict log: ... 10.244.29.231:59052 -> 10.244.2.99:10162 tcp SYN # post-DNAT -- to-endpoint: SYN/ACK SrcIP=10.105.148.60 -> 10.244.29.231 # outer rev-DNAT OK -- to-overlay: 1594-byte DF (TLS ClientHello) 10.244.29.231 -> 10.244.2.99 -- to-endpoint: ICMPv4 DestinationUnreachable(FragmentationNeeded) mtu=1280 SrcIP=10.105.148.60 -> 10.244.29.231, state related # outer translated ... client retransmits the same 1594-byte segment, same ICMP repeats, connection stalls until the peer closes (~10 s) ``` No drop events are emitted (`cilium-dbg monitor -t drop` stays silent for these flows) — nothing is dropped by the datapath, the PMTU signal is just unusable by the client. ## Anything else? - Works: same flow addressed to the backend **pod IP** (PMTUD functions normally). - Workaround we deployed: TCP MSS clamping (`iptables -t mangle -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN -j TCPMSS --set-mss 1240`) inside the proxy pods, so no oversized segments are ever produced and the broken ICMP path is never needed. - `bpf-lb-sock=true` should also avoid it (socket tuple would match the embedded packet), but that is a cluster-wide datapath change. - Possibly related: #39773, #46993. ## Cilium Users Document - [ ] Are you a user of Cilium? Please add yourself to the Users doc ## Code of Conduct - [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct

signal.title: Migrate `pkg/node/types.Node` to `netip`
signal.text: ### Is your proposed feature related to a problem? This issue is a subissue of the larger netip migration (#24246). The scope is migrating [`pkg/node/types.Node`](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/080b189e9f7b97af40b8e74632a15f8551539b9a/pkg/node/types/node.go#L39)'s fields from `net.IP` and `*cidr.CIDR` to their [netip](https://pkg.go.dev/net/netip) equivalents. ## The problem: `Node` is a kvstore wire contract `Node` implements `store.Key` and is serialized to the kvstore with `json.Marshal` ([`Node.Marshal`](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/080b189e9f7b97af40b8e74632a15f8551539b9a/pkg/node/types/node.go#L476-L479)), then shared across independently-upgraded agents and, via kvstoremesh, across clustermesh clusters. Its JSON is therefore a cross-version, cross-cluster wire contract, and the fields have no `json` tags: they serialize under their Go names. The problem is specific to the `*cidr.CIDR` fields. `cidr.CIDR` embeds `*net.IPNet` and neither type defines any JSON marshaler, so `net.IPNet` falls back to default struct marshaling of its exported fields and because `net.IPMask` is a `[]byte` with no `MarshalText`, the mask is base64-encoded. In practice, this means a `*cidr.CIDR` for `10.244.1.0/24` currently serializes to JSON as `{"IP":"10.244.1.0","Mask":"////AA=="}` while the equivalent `netip.Prefix` would serialize to the `"10.244.1.0/24"` JSON string because `netip.Prefix` implements [`MarshalText`](https://pkg.go.dev/net/netip#Prefix.MarshalText) which `json.Marshal` falls back to. A naive migration replacing the `*cidr.CIDR` with `netip.Prefix` would cause issues during upgrade as their JSON serialized formats are not compatible. A new node emitting `"10.244.1.0/24"` could not be deserialized by an old agent expecting the `{"IP":...,"Mask":...}` form and vice-versa. Note: the good news is that the `net.IP` fields do not have this issue as this type does implement [`MarshalText`](https://pkg.go.dev/net#IP.MarshalText) and so they are fully compatible with `netip.Addr`: * net.IP -> `"10.0.0.5"` * netip.Addr -> `"10.0.0.5"` * nil net.IP -> `""` * zero netip.Addr -> `""` Example: ``` $ kubectl exec cilium-agent-9vxhn -c cilium-agent -- cilium-dbg kvstore get cilium/state/nodes/v1/CLUSTER_NAME/NODE_NAME Creating etcd client Connecting to etcd server... New lease successfully acquired Starting watcher Successfully listed keys before starting watcher Initial etcd connection established Starting to watch prefix cilium/state/nodes/v1/CLUSTER_NAME/NODE_NAME => {"Name":"NODE_NAME","Cluster":"CLUSTER_NAME","IPAddresses":[{"Type":"InternalIP","IP":"10.16.60.112"},{"Type":"CiliumInternalIP","IP":"10.19.193.137"}],"IPv4AllocCIDR":{"IP":"10.19.193.128","Mask":"////8A=="},"IPv4SecondaryAllocCIDRs":null,"IPv6AllocCIDR":null,"IPv6SecondaryAllocCIDRs":null,"IPv4HealthIP":"","IPv6HealthIP":"","IPv4IngressIP":"","IPv6IngressIP":"","ClusterID":1,"Source":"local","EncryptionKey":0,"Labels":{"beta.kubernetes.io/arch":"amd64","beta.kubernetes.io/instance-type":"n2d-standard-8","beta.kubernetes.io/os":"linux","disk-type.gke.io/hyperdisk-throughput":"true","disk-type.gke.io/pd-balanced":"true","disk-type.gke.io/pd-extreme":"true","disk-type.gke.io/pd-ssd":"true","disk-type.gke.io/pd-standard":"true","failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/region":"europe-west3","failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/zone":"europe-west3-c","kubernetes.io/arch":"amd64","kubernetes.io/hostname":"NODE_NAME","kubernetes.io/os":"linux","node.kubernetes.io/instance-type":"n2d-standard-8","topology.gke.io/zone":"europe-west3-c","topology.kubernetes.io/region":"europe-west3","topology.kubernetes.io/zone":"europe-west3-c"},"Annotations":{},"NodeIdentity":1,"WireguardPubKey":"","BootID":"84119f79-c8d9-455a-9a12-d216cb98fbd3"} ``` Or pretty-printed: ```json { "Name": "NODE_NAME", "Cluster": "CLUSTER_NAME", "IPAddresses": [ { "Type": "InternalIP", "IP": "10.16.60.112" }, { "Type": "CiliumInternalIP", "IP": "10.19.193.137" } ], "IPv4AllocCIDR": { "IP": "10.19.193.128", "Mask": "////8A==" }, "IPv4SecondaryAllocCIDRs": null, "IPv6AllocCIDR": null, "IPv6SecondaryAllocCIDRs": null, "IPv4HealthIP": "", "IPv6HealthIP": "", "IPv4IngressIP": "", "IPv6IngressIP": "", "ClusterID": 1, "Source": "local", "EncryptionKey": 0, "Labels": { "beta.kubernetes.io/arch": "amd64", "beta.kubernetes.io/instance-type": "n2d-standard-8", "beta.kubernetes.io/os": "linux", "disk-type.gke.io/hyperdisk-throughput": "true", "disk-type.gke.io/pd-balanced": "true", "disk-type.gke.io/pd-extreme": "true", "disk-type.gke.io/pd-ssd": "true", "disk-type.gke.io/pd-standard": "true", "failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/region": "europe-west3", "failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/zone": "europe-west3-c", "kubernetes.io/arch": "amd64", "kubernetes.io/hostname": "NODE_NAME", "kubernetes.io/os": "linux", "node.kubernetes.io/instance-type": "n2d-standard-8", "topology.gke.io/zone": "europe-west3-c", "topology.kubernetes.io/region": "europe-west3", "topology.kubernetes.io/zone": "europe-west3-c" }, "Annotations": {}, "NodeIdentity": 1, "WireguardPubKey": "", "BootID": "84119f79-c8d9-455a-9a12-d216cb98fbd3" } ``` The above node example comes from a cluster using [kubernetes IPAM mode](https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/network/concepts/ipam/kubernetes/) in IPv4-only mode. We can confirm that because `IPv4AllocCIDR` is set and `IPv6AllocCIDR` isn't. We can also observe how those two `*cidr.CIDR` each get serialized: `IPv4AllocCIDR` gets the IP/Mask fields described above (`"IP":"10.19.193.128","Mask":"////8A=="}`) while `IPv6AllocCIDR` is the literal `null` since `Node` fields don't set either [`omitempty`](https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/json#Marshal) or [`omitzero`](https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/json#Marshal) so they all always get serialized, even if `nil`. ### Describe the feature you'd like ## Proposed approach: transitional wrapper with dual-format marshaling The proposed solution is to introduce a transitional field type (e.g. `pkg/node/types.Prefix`) that embeds the end-state `ip.Prefix` (so we converge on the canonical wrapper and don't migrate twice) but with custom JSON Marshal/Unmarshal methods: * `MarshalJSON` keeps emitting the legacy `{"IP","Mask"}` object (byte-exact), and `null` for an unset value (matching a nil `*cidr.CIDR`). * `UnmarshalJSON` accepts both the (current) legacy object and the target string form, plus `null`. ### Rollout lifecycle 1. Release N (1.21): read both formats, write legacy. Old peers keep working. 2. Release N+1 (1.22): once all supported versions can read both, flip `MarshalJSON` to write the string form. 3. Release N+2 (1.23): drop the wrapper, the fields become plain `ip.Prefix`, whose inherited `MarshalText` already emits the string form. ### Notify relevant community channels _No response_ ### (Optional) Describe your proposed solution _No response_

signal.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [X] I have searched the existing issues ### Version equal or higher than v1.16.0 and lower than v1.17.0 ### What happened? I'm having troubles talking onto LoadBalancer services from outside "world" when user is on lower MTU than cluster's. It seems like ICMP "fragmentation needed" is not delivered to the pod. Instead it loops on k8s host until its TTL exceedes. I've seen lots of issues around this but it LOOKS like it SHOULD (https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/12854 https://github.com/industrialdiscipline/cilium/commit/07edf550cab7f865ef83522061256183a803109e) be solved. Unfortunately not for me. Interesting is I can't see any drops of ICMP using cilium monitor. TBH I'm pretty new to cilium so I'm a little confused how to debug this any further. So I've tried to use tcpdump all around and draw a scheme of what I think is happening where red line is what is **wrong** and dotted lines are what SHOULD happen. I hope it makes sense. Cilium is installed with helm using these values: ### How can we reproduce the issue? * Install cilium with helm using this values: ``` bpf: hostLegacyRouting: false masquerade: true cluster: name: <CUT> cni: customConf: false uninstall: false ipam: mode: cluster-pool operator: clusterPoolIPv4PodCIDRList: - 10.98.0.0/16 clusterPoolIPv6PodCIDRList: - fd11:1111:1111::/112 operator: replicas: 1 unmanagedPodWatcher: restart: true policyEnforcementMode: default routingMode: tunnel tunnelProtocol: vxlan kubeProxyReplacement: true k8sServiceHost: <CUT> k8sServicePort: 6443 hubble: relay: enabled: false ui: <CUT> ipv4: enabled: true ipv6: enabled: true pmtuDiscovery: enabled: true fragmentTracking: true ``` * create a ciliumloadbalancerippools * create a service of type LoadBalancer, let it allocate IP * Have a machine with lower MTU somewhere else. signal.title: bpf: don't reclassify an already reverse-NATed service reply
signal.text: - [X] For first time contributors, read [Submitting a pull request] - [X] All code is covered by unit and/or runtime tests where feasible. - [X] All commits contain a well written commit description including a title, description and a `Fixes: #XXX` line if the commit addresses a particular GitHub issue. - [X] If your commit description contains a `Fixes: <commit-id>` tag, then please add the commit author[s] as reviewer[s] to this issue. - [X] All commits are signed off. See the section [Developer’s Certificate of Origin] - [X] Provide a title or release-note blurb suitable for the release notes. - [X] Disclose use of machine learning models (including LLMs and other generative AI) in accordance with the [Cilium AI Policy], and indicate the rating using [AI Influence Level]. - [X] Thanks for contributing! <!-- Description of change --> On netkit + endpointRoutes + per-packet LB, a service reply is evaluated twice on the client's ingress path. The first pass matches conntrack and reverse-NATs the source to the service address; the packet is then re-delivered and evaluated again, now carrying an address that doesn't match the backend-keyed CT entry, and gets classified CT_NEW. This produces a spurious CT entry, a false Hubble flow showing the client as its own destination on an ephemeral port, and, with an ingress policy on the client, Policy denied drops of established connections' replies. Set a flag on ctx->tc_index after lb{4,6}_rev_nat() reverse-NATs a CT_REPLY packet; cil_to_container() reads and clears it on re-entry and delivers directly instead of re-running ingress. tc_index is used because it's the only per-packet state that survives the re-entry: CB_DELIVERY_FLAGS is cleared by bpf_clear_meta() and skb->mark is consumed by inherit_identity_from_host(), both confirmed via cilium-dbg monitor -v with Debug/DebugLB enabled. Fixes: #47913 ```release-note bpf: fix spurious CT_NEW reclassification of service replies on netkit with endpoint routes and per-packet load balancing, which caused incorrect Hubble flows and could drop replies to established connections under an ingress CiliumNetworkPolicy. ``` This PR was prepared with AIL:4. I personally validated the resulting network flows with and without policies, both visually via Hubble and by testing the affected applications. I could not find an existing test in the suite combining netkit + endpointRoutes + per-packet LB. Every netkit test that I found has per_packet_lb=0. Three tests enable per-packet LB and exercise bpf_lxc (skip_lb_xlate_lrp_per_packet_lb.c, tc_nodeport_lb_fragments.h, tc_lb_external_ips.h), but all three are netkit=0, endpoint_routes=0. The problem is easily reproducible (see #47913) and the fix is only a few simple lines, so building out a full test harness for netkit=1, endpoint_routes=1 seems disproportionate in this case, and I don't have the background in the code to know that the test case would be right. It was very obvious that the fix addressed the problem without obviously creating new problems (via Hubble UI, policies and applications working again).

signal.title: gateway-api: skip proxy_protocol filter for GAMMA CECs
signal.text: Please ensure your pull request adheres to the following guidelines: - [x] For first time contributors, read [Submitting a pull request] - [x] All code is covered by unit and/or runtime tests where feasible. - [x] All commits contain a well written commit description including a title, description and a `Fixes: #XXX` line if the commit addresses a particular GitHub issue. - [ ] If your commit description contains a `Fixes: <commit-id>` tag, then please add the commit author[s] as reviewer[s] to this issue. - [x] All commits are signed off. See the section [Developer's Certificate of Origin] - [x] Provide a title or release-note blurb suitable for the release notes. - [x] Disclose use of machine learning models (including LLMs and other generative AI) in accordance with the [Cilium AI Policy], and indicate the rating using [AI Influence Level]. - [x] Thanks for contributing! --- ## Summary When `gatewayAPI.enableProxyProtocol=true` is set, the Gateway API controller unconditionally appends `envoy.filters.listener.proxy_protocol` to **every** generated `CiliumEnvoyConfig`, including those for GAMMA (east-west, Service-parented) routes. Cilium's BPF datapath redirects packets to Envoy transparently at L3/L4. When Envoy's `proxy_protocol` listener filter reads the first bytes and finds no `PROXY v1/v2` signature, it immediately closes the connection with a TCP RST. This breaks all L7 east-west mesh traffic with no per-route workaround. The fix gates `withProxyProtocol()` on `!m.IsGamma()` to avoid injecting PROXY protocol filters to GAMMA routes. > [!NOTE] > **AI Disclosure (AIL:3):** I identified, reproduced, and traced the root cause on a live EKS cluster. An LLM (Claude Opus 4.6) assisted with code authoring and test writing under my full review. Investigation notes and reproduction logs are available in the linked issue. ## Changes - Gate `withProxyProtocol()` on `!m.IsGamma()` in `listenerMutatorsForPorts` — no new helper needed - Added tests to gate against the issue. Fixes: #47500 ```release-note Fix `proxy_protocol` listener filter incorrectly injected into GAMMA CiliumEnvoyConfigs when `gatewayAPI.enableProxyProtocol` is enabled ``` [AI Influence Level]: https://danielmiessler.com/blog/ai-influence-level-ail [Cilium AI Policy]: https://github.com/cilium/community/blob/main/AI-POLICY.md [Developer's Certificate of Origin]: https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/contributing/development/contributing_guide/#dev-coo [Submitting a pull request]: https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/contributing/development/contributing_guide/#submitting-a-pull-request
